title: The Sale Happens in December. The Cost of Taking It Back Lands in February.
linkedin:
Christmas trading is about to post the best month of the year on your profit and loss.

A chunk of that margin is already scheduled to reverse in February.

Gift buying creates the same pattern every year. Wrong sizes, duplicate presents, a gift that wasn't quite right for the person who opened it. All of it comes back as a return or exchange through January and into February.

Here's the part that's easy to miss. A refund rarely reverses only the sale price. The payment processing fee is usually non-refundable. Freight is often paid twice. Someone has to inspect, repackage and sometimes remark down the item before it can be resold.

On a $120 jumper sold at a 50 percent margin, the $60 of gross profit it appeared to generate in December can be mostly gone by February once all of that is counted.

The pattern we see across owner-led retail and e-commerce businesses is that December's numbers only tell half the story. The reversal lands in a different month's figures entirely, usually once the owner has already moved on to planning the new year.

The fix isn't complicated. Last year's return rate, by category and channel, is already sitting in the point of sale or e-commerce platform. Apply it to this year's forecast and the return cost becomes a planned line item instead of an unpleasant surprise in February.

Christmas trading is shaping up to be the strongest month of the year for a lot of gift-driven retailers and online stores across Brisbane, the Gold Coast and the wider East Coast. The sales numbers look great right now, and for most businesses they genuinely are.

What is easy to miss is how much of that December margin quietly comes back in January and February. Gift buying creates the same pattern every year: wrong sizes, duplicate presents, a gift that was not quite right for the person who received it. All of it shows up as a return or exchange once the holidays are over.

The part that catches owners out is not the refund itself, it is everything that comes with it. Payment processing fees are often non-refundable even when a sale is reversed, freight is sometimes paid twice, and a returned item frequently has to be resold at a markdown rather than at full price. Added up, a sale that looked solidly profitable in December can be close to break even by the time it is fully wound back.

The businesses that handle this well are the ones who look at last year's actual return rate and build it into this year's Christmas forecast now, rather than being surprised by it in February.
